name: Grotesque sans
region: London, then Germany and the United States
summary: The first sans serifs: plain, heavy letters for posters, with a little contrast, some quirks of width and a two-storey g. Later text cuts such as Akzidenz-Grotesk and Franklin Gothic gave the class a sober, workmanlike voice.

philosophy.core_thesis: A letter without serifs is plain, and the plain letter is the strongest one at a distance.
design_principles: Keep the stroke contrast at 1.1–1.6:1, with a slight thinning where curves meet stems.
Use a two-storey g or a g with a spur, a spurred G and an R with a straight or curved leg.
Let the widths vary: a wide M and W, a narrow S and E, with no strict rule.
Cut the terminals of c, e and s at an angle or close to horizontal, with a moderate aperture.
Hold the x-height at 0.68–0.78 of the cap height.
Set headlines in bold or condensed bold; the grotesque is at its best in heavy weights.
anti_patterns: Pure geometric circles and triangles in the letters
A uniform, optically perfect width for all capitals
Serifs or slabs on any letter

classification.note: The Vox Lineale class has four sub-classes: grotesque, neo-grotesque, geometric and humanist. The grotesque shows more contrast and more quirks than the neo-grotesque.

anatomy.contrast: Low but visible: the thin parts are 0.6–0.9 of the stem; the joins of n and m thin out.
anatomy.stress: Vertical, where the joins show any thinning at all.
anatomy.serifs: None: the strokes end clean, with no serif.
anatomy.terminals: Cut at an angle or close to horizontal on c, e, s and the bowl of a.
anatomy.aperture: Moderate: smaller than in a humanist sans, larger than in a neo-grotesque.
anatomy.key_letters: A two-storey g (often with an ear), a G with a spur, an R with a straight leg, and a square-shouldered a.

metrics.x_height: The x-height is 0.68–0.78 of the cap height and about 0.47–0.53 of the em.
metrics.contrast: The side of the o is 1.1 to 1.6 times as thick as its top.
metrics.width: Medium, with uneven widths between letters; condensed cuts are common.
metrics.figures: Lining figures; tabular in news and timetable cuts.

setting.text_sizes: Set text at 9–11 pt in print and 15–18 px on screen.
setting.display_sizes: Set headlines at 24–144 pt in bold or condensed bold.
setting.leading: Set the leading at 1.35–1.5 for text and 0.95–1.1 for headlines.
setting.tracking: Set 0 to +0.01 em in text, −0.01 to −0.03 em in large headlines, +0.05 em for capitals.
setting.case_and_features: Use capitals and condensed cuts for posters; tabular figures for data.

pairing.rule: Pair it with a serif of the same century, or use one grotesque family in several widths and weights.

pairs.why: The two classes came from the same posters, so the pair feels historically true.
The serif carries the reading, and the grotesque carries the headings and the data.

faces.designer: Pablo Impallari, Rodrigo Fuenzalida, Nhung Nguyen

reference_faces.note: Work Sans takes its forms from early grotesques. The default instance of Libre Franklin in google/fonts is the Thin weight, so the specimen uses Work Sans.

emotion.target_response: Plain strength: the reader feels a direct, honest voice with some character left in it.

avoid_when: The brief asks for a perfectly neutral, systematic face.
The brief asks for warmth or a handwritten feel.

modifiers.how: Even the widths, close the apertures to horizontal terminals, and bring the contrast down to 1.1:1.
Add square slabs and keep the weight; set the headline in capitals.

sources.title: Robert Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style (Hartley & Marks, 4th ed. 2012)
